# Samuggajātaka (Ja 436)

**ID:** Ja 436
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Box

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Samuggajātaka* (Ja 436), titled *The Box* in modern translation, is a narrative of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. Set at Jetavana, the story is delivered by the Buddha to admonish a monk who is discontent with the monastic life and hankering after the worldly pleasures of women [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883]. The Buddha illustrates the unfaithfulness of women and the futility of guarding them through a past-life tale opening with the verse line *Kuto nu āgacchatha* [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883; Cabezón 2017]. In the narrative, an Asura demon (*dānava*) swallows his woman to keep her safe within his belly or carries her in a casket (*samugga*); nevertheless, she engages in secret adultery with a sword-bearing wizard (*vidyādhara*) until a forest ascetic endowed with divine vision (the Bodhisatta) exposes the deception, prompting the demon to cough up the casket [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1883; von Hinüber 1994; Cabezón 2017].

Scholars have noted that the narrative closely resembles motifs found in later world literature, such as the frame story of the *Arabian Nights* [Law 1931]. The jātaka is also celebrated in early Buddhist visual art: it is depicted on the Prasenajit pillar at the Bhārhut stūpa under the epigraphic label *vijapi vijadharo* ("The Vidyādhara Vijapi"), where details such as the wizard's shield and sword scabbard hanging in a tree corroborate the gāthā text [Wood 2005; von Hinüber 1994].

In the Pali tradition, the canonical verses are preserved alongside their commentary in the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [Fausböll 1883]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus reflects this integration, finding 13 matching segments shared between the verse text and the third volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns passages automatically with the Tibetan translation of the *Jātakamālā* (D4150) and the *Saddharmānusmṛtyupasthāna* (D0287-3) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four modern translations of the tale across four languages [SuttaCentral].
